It solves the problem of efficiently estimating radiance by replacing the infinite-dimensional integral with a Gaussian-weighted sum of "surrounding" paths [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the approach approximates the complete path integral by taking into account only the contribution of 'surrounding' paths. It further explains that the expansion of the action results in a Gaussian form (Equation 12 and 13), which gives weights to nearby paths. This process effectively replaces the complex infinite-dimensional integral with a Gaussian-weighted sum (integral) over the parameters of these surrounding paths to estimate radiance properties.

where $(\xi \nabla_{\xi})^2 A$ represents the quadratic form $\vec{\xi}^T \mathbf{H} \vec{\xi}$ derived from the Hessian [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that when parameterizing the family of nearby paths using a vector ξ, the expansion of the action A starts from square terms because A has a global minimum at the MPP. It provides the scalar Taylor expansion $A(0) + (1/2)ξ^2 (∂^2A/∂ξ^2)$ and then generalizes this to the vector case in Equation 13 as $G ~ exp(-A(MPP)) ∫_ξ exp(-(ξ ∇_ξ)² A / 2) dξ$. The term $(ξ ∇_ξ)² A$ in the exponent corresponds to the quadratic form derived from the second-order expansion (Hessian) of the action A with respect to the parameters ξ. Thus, the claim that $(ξ ∇_ξ)² A$ represents the quadratic form derived from the Hessian is supported by the text.
